data.title: Bedside manners
data.description:
Four lessons from electronic renewals that matter as AI enters patient support

Consider a patient receiving a long-term therapy through a drug manufacturer’s assistance programme. As renewal approaches, their insurance details have changed, or their income status has changed. The patient can complete an online form, but the prescriber must confirm another part of the application. Then a secure link expires. The problem is no longer how quickly software processes a form; it is whether someone can recover the case without making both parties begin again.

Patient assistance automation is often evaluated by how many manual steps it removes. That is a useful measure, but an incomplete one. The more revealing test is what happens when a renewal does not follow the expected path: who is alerted, what information travels with the exception and how quickly an accountable person can act.

I worked on the technology integration for an electronic patient assistance programme (ePAP) enrolment and renewal initiative at a US rare-disease company in 2023. The programme design introduced separate digital application paths for patients and prescribers, linked the portal to an existing patient-services environment and supported renewal communications at scale.

It was conventional workflow automation, not AI. Yet it exposed four design decisions that matter even more as AI enters patient support.

1. Design around the people who complete the application

A renewal is not one document completed by one person. Patients, carers, prescribers and support staff have different responsibilities, information and permissions. Moving a paper form online does little if the same information still has to be repeatedly collected or checked by the wrong participant.

Our integration design specified distinct patient and prescriber experiences, with secure links and additional verification for prescribers. It also defined how existing patient details could be retrieved to support the online process. The broader lesson is to divide the workflow according to who can reliably supply or attest to each piece of information. Automation should reduce unnecessary repetition without blurring responsibility for clinical or eligibility-related information.

2. Engineer the failure path before celebrating the happy path

The most instructive design discussions concerned exceptions. What happens if a link expires? If verification fails repeatedly? If an email address is missing or needs updating? The workflow we designed specified status notifications, ways to request replacement links and escalation paths involving support staff. These were not peripheral error messages. They were part of the service.

The same principle applies when an AI tool reads a document, suggests missing information or proposes the next action. A low-confidence extraction or a conflicting answer should not disappear into a dashboard. It needs an explicit handover: the reason for referral, the supporting information, the responsible team and a way to see whether the case was resolved. The system should be designed around recoverability, not an assumption that every transaction will succeed.

3. Return completed information to the operational record

A digital portal can provide an excellent experience while leaving case managers with another silo. Our integration design specified the return of application information to the patient-services environment, including relevant patient, prescriber and consent information and supporting materials. The aim was to keep the operational record usable after the online interaction ended.

For leaders evaluating AI, that is a more demanding requirement than a successful demonstration. Where will a proposed answer, a validated field or an unresolved exception appear? Can staff identify its origin and correct it without re-entering everything? If the output is disconnected from the record people rely on, automation has merely relocated administrative work.

4. Keep accountability separate from automation

Electronic applications can collect information and apply predefined validation steps. They should not be mistaken for a complete, independently accountable determination of a patient’s eligibility. Where rules are ambiguous, information conflicts or supporting documents are incomplete, people need a clear path to review the case and explain what happens next.

That principle has a regulatory dimension, although obligations differ by programme and country. UK rules on solely automated significant decisions include safeguards such as the ability to obtain human intervention and contest a decision. In the EU, certain direct interactions with AI systems trigger transparency obligations. Neither framework should be casually applied to a US assistance programme; both reinforce why the boundary between automated processing and consequential decisions deserves deliberate design.

My subsequent review of AI in healthcare CRM examined opportunities from automation alongside the need for privacy, transparency and responsible implementation. The practical question I would bring to any new tool is simpler: when it cannot complete a task safely, can it transfer the work to a person with enough context to act?

Measure the handover, not just the throughput

A 2026 Guidehouse survey reported a 23-point decline in pharmaceutical leaders using third-party hub services, reflecting a shift towards more internal and hybrid patient-support models. Whether services are delivered by a manufacturer, a partner or both, someone must own the unresolved case. The technology cannot settle that accountability on its own.

I would therefore track completion time, and also expired-link recovery, cases awaiting review, information that must be requested again and the time between an exception and a human response. These are recommended measures, not documented outcomes from the 2023 initiative. They test the quality of the experience when automation meets its limits.

Return to the patient facing renewal. Success is not simply receiving a faster online form. It is completing the right steps once, knowing what remains outstanding and having a real route forward when something goes wrong. That is the standard that patient assistance automation, and any AI layered on top of it, should be built to meet.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jaymin Sutarwala is Associate Director, CRM Strategy & Operations at United Therapeutics. His work spans patient-services technology, healthcare CRM integrations and pharmaceutical workflow automation

data.title: ViiV wins CHMP backing for paediatric HIV drugs
data.description:
ViiV Healthcare has received positive opinions from the European Medicines Agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) recommending expanded use of Tivicay and Dovato in younger children living with HIV across the EU.

The recommendations are aimed at addressing ongoing treatment gaps in paediatric HIV care. According to ViiV, only 55% of children living with HIV globally received antiretroviral therapy in 2024, while around half of untreated infants with HIV die before reaching two years of age.

The CHMP recommended extending the indication for Tivicay (dolutegravir) dispersible tablets for use in HIV-infected adults, adolescents, children and term neonates from birth weighing at least 2kg when used with other antiretroviral medicines.

If approved, ViiV said Tivicay would become the first second-generation integrase inhibitor available in the EU for eligible newborns.

The committee also recommended approval of a new dispersible tablet formulation of Dovato (dolutegravir/lamivudine) for children aged at least three months and weighing between 6kg and less than 25kg. An extension to the existing film-coated tablet indication for children weighing at least 20kg was also recommended.

If approved, Dovato could become the first single-tablet, two-drug treatment option for eligible younger children living with HIV in the EU.

Jean van Wyk, Chief Medical Officer at ViiV Healthcare, said: “Children living with HIV require lifelong care, making continued innovation essential. If approved, Tivicay would become the first second-generation integrase inhibitor to offer eligible newborns dolutegravir-based treatment, while Dovato would bring the first single tablet, two-drug regimen option to eligible younger children.”

He added: “These positive CHMP opinions mark an important step towards expanding age-appropriate, INSTI-based treatment options for children and advancing our goal of offering greater choice in HIV care, so more people living with HIV can benefit from innovative treatment options at every stage of life.”

The applications were supported by data from the IMPAACT 2023, Penta-21 and DANCE studies. European Commission decisions are expected in the first quarter of 2027.

data.title: Tryngolza approved in EU for severe hypertriglyceridaemia
data.description:
The European Commission has approved Tryngolza (olezarsen) as an adjunct to diet and other lipid-lowering therapies for adults with severe hypertriglyceridaemia (sHTG) with fasting triglyceride levels of at least 880 mg/dL (10 mmol/L).

The approval makes Tryngolza the first and only RNA-targeted therapy authorised in the EU for patients with sHTG at this threshold. The decision follows a positive opinion from the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) in October and expands the medicine’s existing indication for familial chylomicronaemia syndrome into a broader patient population.

The approval was based on data from the phase 3 CORE and CORE2 studies, sponsored by Ionis Pharmaceuticals and conducted with the TIMI Study Group. A pre-specified analysis of patients with baseline triglyceride levels of at least 880 mg/dL showed the treatment reduced triglyceride levels by up to 73% after six months compared with placebo, with benefits maintained for 12 months.

A pooled analysis of the CORE and CORE2 studies also showed an 83% reduction in adjudicated acute pancreatitis events over 12 months compared with placebo.

Approximately 700,000 people across the EU’s five largest markets are estimated to have triglyceride levels of at least 880 mg/dL and are therefore considered at high risk of developing acute pancreatitis.

Erik S.G. Stroes, Professor of Vascular Medicine at Amsterdam UMC, said: “Acute pancreatitis is a potentially life-threatening medical emergency that may require intensive care admission and prolonged hospitalisation.”

He added: “Some patients experience permanent organ damage and lasting effects on their quality of life. There is an unmet need for patients with sHTG for new, effective therapies to help reduce the risk of acute pancreatitis.”

Lydia Abad-Franch, Head of R&D and Medical Affairs and Chief Medical Officer at Sobi, commented: “The European Commission’s approval of Tryngolza for the treatment of sHTG is an important step forward for patients in Europe who remain at increased risk of acute pancreatitis despite diet and existing lipid-lowering therapies.”

She continued: “The EC decision marks meaningful progress for eligible patients living with sHTG.”

Brett P. Monia, Chief Executive Officer of Ionis, explained: “This approval reflects the potential of RNA-targeted medicines to address serious conditions such as sHTG. We are proud to work with our long-standing partner Sobi to bring Tryngolza to people in need across the EU.”

data.title: Still Time to Secure Your Pass for MAD World Summit 2026
data.description:
There is still time to secure your place at MAD World Summit 2026, taking place on Thursday 26 November at Convene, 155 Bishopsgate, London.

Bringing together some of the biggest names in business, the ninth annual summit will welcome leaders and professionals from organisations including HSBC UK, Disney, Burberry and BAE Systems, alongside 38 expert speakers from across workplace wellbeing, HR and organisational culture. Speakers include representatives from BNP Paribas, Ofcom and The Crown Estate, offering valuable insights and practical advice on creating healthier, happier and more productive workplaces.

With workplace wellbeing firmly on the business agenda, MAD World 2026 will explore the challenges facing today’s organisations and how employers can turn their wellbeing strategies into meaningful action.

Key topics on this year’s programme include:

– Tackling workplace burnout: Understanding the causes of burnout and building systems that support sustainable wellbeing rather than contributing to the problem.

– The future of work and AI: Exploring how AI is reshaping the workplace, its impact on employees and what organisations can do to support their people through change.

– Building inclusive workplace cultures: Addressing neurodiversity, inclusion and the different wellbeing needs of today’s workforce.

– Supporting the next generation: Understanding what early-career professionals need to thrive, develop and build sustainable careers.

– Mental health as a business priority: Examining how organisations can make the case for workplace mental health and connect wellbeing with business performance.

– Psychosocial risks and workplace culture: Identifying emerging workplace challenges and developing practical approaches to creating healthier working environments.

The programme also features keynote presentations, interactive workshops, panel discussions and dedicated networking opportunities, giving attendees the chance to share experiences, exchange ideas and connect with like-minded professionals.

Whether you’re looking to strengthen your organisation’s wellbeing strategy, gain fresh perspectives on workplace culture or learn from those leading change across major organisations, MAD World Summit 2026 offers a valuable opportunity to take away practical insights and inspiration.

Book your MAD World Summit 2026 pass here: https://madworldsummit.com/delegate-pass/

View the live agenda here: https://madworldsummit.com/mad-world-agenda-2026/

data.title: Sepalna approved in Europe for ovarian cancer
data.description:
The European Commission has approved Sepalna (senaparib) as a monotherapy maintenance treatment for adults with advanced epithelial high-grade ovarian, fallopian tube or primary peritoneal cancer whose disease has responded either completely or partially following first-line platinum-based chemotherapy.

The approval covers patients with FIGO stage 3 and 4 disease and follows a positive opinion from the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) in September 2026. The decision, granted on 12 November 2026, marks a significant regulatory milestone for the treatment in Europe.

Pharmanovia and IMPACT Therapeutics announced the authorisation, which applies across the European Union. Pharmanovia holds exclusive regional development and commercialisation rights for senaparib across 66 countries, including the UK, Norway, Iceland, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Australia, New Zealand and countries in the Middle East and North Africa.

Senaparib, developed by IMPACT Therapeutics, is a targeted anti-cancer therapy. The approval was supported by evidence from the phase 3 FLAMES study, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving patients with newly diagnosed advanced ovarian cancer responding to first-line platinum-based chemotherapy, regardless of BRCA mutation status.

At a median follow-up of 48.5 months, the study showed median progression-free survival of 38.7 months in patients receiving senaparib compared with 13.6 months in the placebo group. Benefits were observed in both BRCA-mutated and BRCA wild-type patient populations.

Updated safety data from 403 patients showed that 5.6% of those treated with senaparib discontinued treatment because of treatment-emergent adverse events. The most common adverse events included anaemia, neutropenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, increased transaminases, weight gain, nausea and abdominal pain.

No treatment-emergent adverse events resulted in death.

Stephan Eder, Chief Executive Officer of Pharmanovia, said: “The European Commission’s approval of Sepalna represents an important milestone for patients with advanced ovarian cancer and for our growing oncology portfolio.”

He added: “We congratulate our partner IMPACT Therapeutics on this significant achievement, reflecting years of dedicated research and clinical development.”

Eder continued: “Our focus at Pharmanovia is now on preparing for the introduction of Sepalna across Europe and working towards making this treatment available to eligible patients.”

data.title: Lexeo reports positive phase 1/2 data for LX2020
data.description:
Lexeo Therapeutics has reported positive interim results from its ongoing phase 1/2 HEROIC-PKP2 clinical trial evaluating LX2020 in patients with PKP2 arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (PKP2-ACM), alongside a regulatory update that may support an accelerated approval pathway.

The company said LX2020 was generally well tolerated across 10 participants treated in the study, with no clinically significant complement activation observed and no study discontinuations reported.

Data from the high-dose cohorts showed an 80% mean reduction in non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT) and a 44% mean reduction in premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) at the latest assessment compared with baseline.

Lexeo said six of seven participants in the high-dose groups demonstrated improvement in NSVT burden, while five of seven showed reductions in PVC burden. Five participants also reported symptom improvement relative to baseline.

The company reported preliminary evidence of stabilisation or improvement in cardiac function in most participants receiving the higher dose, based on cardiac MRI assessments.

In discussions with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Lexeo said the agency was open to the use of guideline-defined NSVT as a primary surrogate endpoint in a pivotal study designed to support accelerated approval.

R. Nolan Townsend, Chief Executive Officer of Lexeo Therapeutics, said: “These data further strengthen our confidence in LX2020 and its potential to address the underlying biology of PKP2-ACM. The magnitude and consistency of NSVT reduction far exceed what available therapies have historically achieved, underscoring how LX2020 could meaningfully improve outcomes for individuals with PKP2-ACM.”

He added: “Our regulatory discussions also provide important clarity on the path forward, including the FDA’s openness to the use of NSVT as a primary endpoint in a planned pivotal study given the well-established association between NSVT and sustained, life-threatening arrhythmic risk.”

Walker Frahm, Chief Executive Officer of the Foundation for Inherited Arrhythmias, explained: “Our community has waited a long time for treatments that might address the underlying cause of this disease. Early results like these give ACM families reason to hope for better, more targeted care.”

Lexeo expects to finalise the design of its pivotal study during the first half of 2027 and initiate the trial in the second half of the year.

data.title: Neurizon reaches new HEALEY ALS trial milestone
data.description:
Neurizon Therapeutics has announced that the first participant in Regimen I of the phase 2/3 HEALEY ALS Platform Trial has completed the 36-week randomised controlled trial phase and moved into the Active Treatment Extension (ATE).

The milestone follows the completion of enrolment in July 2026, when 250 participants were recruited across 78 clinical sites in the US. Under the extension protocol, eligible participants can continue in the study and receive investigational treatment with NUZ-001.

According to the company, the ATE is designed to generate additional long-term safety, tolerability, functional and biomarker data beyond that collected during the placebo-controlled phase. Participants will continue to undergo assessments including ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised measurements, respiratory function monitoring and quality-of-life evaluations.

Blood and urine biomarker testing, including neurofilament light chain assessments, will also continue throughout the extension period.

Neurizon said the additional observations are expected to complement data gathered during the randomised phase and contribute to the wider clinical evidence package supporting the development of NUZ-001. Treatment assignments will remain blinded during the extension.

The company noted that Regimen I enrolled all 250 participants in around five months, which it described as the fastest enrolment in ALS trial history.

The update also follows recent feedback from the US FDA indicating that positive results from the HEALEY ALS Platform Trial may support a traditional approval pathway, with Regimen I potentially serving as a single registrational study for NUZ-001, subject to regulatory requirements being met.

Dr Chris Bremer, Chief Executive Officer of Neurizon, said: “The first participant entering the Active Treatment Extension is an important milestone for Regimen I and reflects the continued progress of our clinical development program.

“For people living with ALS, a progressive disease with limited treatment options, advancing research into potential new therapies is critically important. We are grateful to the participants who continue to contribute to this research, and to their families and clinical teams for their commitment.”

Merit Cudkowicz, Executive Director of the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute and Director of the Healey & AMG Center for ALS, explained: “We believe strongly that it is critical to design clinical trials to get clear results in the shortest time period.

“After enrolling 250 participants in 5 months, we are excited to now have taken this next step in Regimen I of the HEALEY ALS Platform Trial.”

data.title: Enterprise secures EMA orphan status for CF therapy
data.description:
Enterprise Therapeutics has been granted orphan medicinal product designation by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) Committee for Orphan Medicinal Products (COMP) for ETD001, its investigational treatment for cystic fibrosis (CF).

The Brighton-based biopharmaceutical company said the designation follows positive results from a phase 2 clinical trial of ETD001, an inhaled epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) blocker designed to improve lung function by enhancing mucus clearance and reducing airway obstruction.

According to the company, the EMA COMP concluded that ETD001 met the criteria for orphan designation based on the rarity of cystic fibrosis and the therapy’s potential to deliver clinically relevant benefits. The opinion also recognised the potential of the treatment for people who are not eligible for CFTR modulator therapy.

The recommendation was supported by clinical data from the phase 2 ET-ENAC-03 study, which indicated improvements in lung function.

Orphan medicinal product designation in the EU provides a range of incentives for developers of treatments targeting rare diseases, including market exclusivity after approval.

Dr John Ford, CEO of Enterprise Therapeutics, said: “Orphan drug designation represents an important regulatory milestone for the ETD001 programme and for Enterprise Therapeutics. The decision by the EMA reflects the continued need for additional treatment options for people with cystic fibrosis, particularly those who are not able to benefit from CFTR modulators.”

He added: “We look forward to continuing the development of ETD001 in CF as well as other mucus congestion related respiratory diseases.”

Annabella Amatulli, Head of Regulatory Affairs at Enterprise Therapeutics, explained: “Our regulatory strategy supports our global development plan for ETD001, aligned with our goal to provide improved therapeutic options for people with cystic fibrosis. The EMA’s orphan drug designation further validates the strength of the programme’s scientific rationale and outcomes of the phase 2 clinical trial.”

Cystic fibrosis affects an estimated 100,000 people worldwide and is associated with reduced life expectancy. The disease is characterised by impaired mucociliary clearance and mucus congestion in the lungs, leading to recurring infection, inflammation and progressive declines in lung function.

data.title: Updated data bolster pancreatic cancer programme
data.description:
Revolution Medicines has reported updated phase 1/2 data showing that its RASONQUE (daraxonrasib) combination regimen continued to deliver deep and durable responses in patients with first-line metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC).

The latest findings from the RMC-GI-102 study were presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR (ENA) Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain. Results support the ongoing phase 3 RASolute 303 trial in treatment-naïve metastatic pancreatic cancer.

As of 28 September 2026, 61 patients had received RASONQUE plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel (GnP) in the first-line metastatic PDAC cohort, with a median follow-up of 18.3 months.

The updated analysis showed a confirmed objective response rate of 60.7%, including complete responses in 8.2% of patients. The disease control rate was 90.2%, while the median duration of response was 11.1 months.

Median progression-free survival reached 12.8 months and the estimated 12-month overall survival rate was 76.6%. The safety profile was reported to be consistent with previous observations for both RASONQUE and GnP.

Dr Wungki Park, medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and investigator for the study, said: “With longer follow-up and a larger patient population, we are seeing a notable combination of high response rates, including deep complete responses, and durable disease control, with median progression-free survival exceeding one year.”

He added: “The emerging survival signal is meaningful and is estimated at 76.6% for patients to be alive at one year. Taken together, these findings provide a compelling rationale to further evaluate daraxonrasib as a potential first-line treatment option.”

The programme recently received FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designation for RASONQUE plus GnP in this setting.

Dr Alan Sandler, chief development officer of Revolution Medicines, explained: “People with treatment-naïve metastatic pancreatic cancer urgently need more effective treatment options, given the limited clinical benefit of current chemotherapy regimens.”

He added: “The durability of treatment shown with these updated phase 1/2 results is particularly encouraging and supports the ongoing phase 3 RASolute 303 trial.”

data.title: SRD Search launches on VIDAL with first pharmaceutical company – Pfizer
data.description:
Datapharm, the company behind emc, the UK’s trusted source of regulatory-approved medicines information, has announced the launch of its SRD Search functionality on VIDAL in France.

Pfizer is the first manufacturer to make its Scientific Response Documents (SRDs) available to French healthcare professionals (HCPs) through the service. Since going live in August 2026, Pfizer has published 373 French SRDs covering nine of its brands.

France is the third market for SRD Search, following the UK on emc and Germany on Rote Liste. Fourteen pharmaceutical companies currently use the service across the three markets, with take-up continuing to grow.

Search data from the UK and Germany has already shown that HCP behaviour differs by market. In Germany, nine in ten searches are a single word and more than half are typed in English rather than German. In both markets, a significant share of searches happens outside the hours a Medical Information service is typically staffed.

The launch on VIDAL marks the start of building the same level of insight for France. Participating manufacturers receive analytics reports showing what French HCPs search for, when they search and which questions go unanswered, helping them refine their SRD content for the French market.

Rob Morgan, Chief Executive Officer, Datapharm, said: “Healthcare professionals need answers they can trust, yet increasingly the first answer they see comes from a tool that cannot distinguish a verified response from an invented one. Manufacturers have already done the hard work of writing and reviewing these documents. SRD Search puts that trusted content where French HCPs already look, at any hour. Launching on VIDAL with Pfizer is an important step in expanding access to trusted medicine information across Europe, and the beginning of understanding how French HCPs search.”

Aqid Iqbal, Europe and Canada Medical Information Operations Manager, Pfizer, said: “Expanding access to Pfizer Medical Information through VIDAL is an important step in our Medical Information strategy of easing access and expanding reach. We are proud that Pfizer is the first manufacturer to make Scientific Response Documents available through this new service on VIDAL. By making trusted Pfizer Scientific Response Documents available through a resource healthcare professionals in France already use, we are enabling greater self-service access to medical information, where and when it is needed. This collaboration builds on our work to bring trusted scientific information closer to healthcare professionals through established digital channels, helping ensure that the science behind our breakthroughs is supported by accessible medical information for those caring for patients.”

Ferran Portella, Managing Director of VIDAL Group’s Medical Knowledge Solutions division, said: “VIDAL’s role is to provide French healthcare professionals with accurate and reliable information on medicines. SRD Search extends what they can find on vidal.fr with approved, in-depth responses from manufacturers, accessible 24/7 whenever they need to make a prescription decision. We are pleased to welcome Pfizer as the first manufacturer on the service.”

Issued by Datapharm Ltd, Cassini Court, Randalls Way, Leatherhead KT22 7TW, on 16 November 2026
